claims.text: The proposed baseline is a lightweight, single-phase HEA with no deliberately added oxide-promoting element or Cr.
A low concentration of added Cr promotes formation of a coherent, continuous, protective Cr-based oxide film at high temperature.
The Cr-based surface layer may contain Cr2O3 and CrNbO4.
At high temperature, Cr diffuses outward toward the alloy surface.
Surface Cr reacts with oxygen to form an oxide film.
A continuous Cr-based oxide layer limits further oxidation.
The Cr-derived protective film reduces corrosive attack.
The Cr-based oxide film stabilizes the alloy microstructure and its dislocation structures.
Oxide-film-mediated stabilization preserves or enhances mechanical strength after high-temperature exposure.
Low-level Cr addition does not significantly increase alloy density.
Cr addition permits the alloy to combine low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance simultaneously.
Relative to the Cr-free baseline, the Cr-doped alloy will have lower oxidation weight gain.
Increasing Cr can raise pitting potential and lower corrosion current density.
Excessive Cr may cause segregation that diminishes or reverses the benefits.
Excessive Cr may form brittle intermetallic phases.
Above approximately 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3.
The hypothesized benefits cease when the protective oxide cannot form or is destroyed by extreme temperature or aggressive chemical conditions.
Acid-solution corrosion tests and oxidation near 1000 °C in oxygen-rich atmospheres mimic aerospace and rail-transport service conditions.
A limited amount of Cr can be insufficient to form a continuous protective oxide layer, making oxidation improvement indiscernible.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis asserts that a low Cr concentration produces a coherent, continuous protective oxide, whereas the identified conflicting evidence reports that limited Cr was insufficient to form a continuous layer and produced no discernible improvement.

Adverse effects at higher Cr content are presented as an expected boundary where the hypothesis should cease to hold, but the falsification rule also treats those same higher-Cr adverse effects as falsifying the hypothesis.

The primary oxidation test is specified at about 1000 °C, while the boundary warns that volatile CrO3 may arise above about 900 °C; the intended valid Cr range at the test temperature is not resolved.
